Solarpunk

The visual side of solarpunk, a speculative-fiction and activist movement named in 2008 that imagines ecologically sustainable futures as the inverse of cyberpunk. Its aesthetic took shape on Tumblr from 2014: bright greens and blues, sunlight as a motif, plants that grow over buildings, visible solar and wind technology, and Art Nouveau curves and stained glass. This record covers that illustrative and graphic core. The fiction, the politics, and green architecture are treated as related branches.

Hopeful / Sunlit / Verdant / Communal / Handmade

Visual grammar

  • Plants grown into technology. Vines, trees, and gardens grow on roofs, balconies, and towers. Solar panels, wind turbines, and sails sit in plain view among them, and people garden, cycle, and build. Technology is visible and repairable, not hidden in a sealed box.
  • Sunlit greens, sky, and gold. Bright leaf and moss green, sky and water blue, and sun yellow or gold on white or warm cream. The colours are clear and bright, not neon and not muted to earth tones. The Aesthetics Wiki gives green, yellow, blue, and white.
  • Arches and stained-glass panes. Arched windows, domes, and greenhouses frame the scene. Their glazing is split into leaded panes, and the solar panel itself is drawn as stained glass: a grid of cells in green, gold, and blue.
  • Open, layered, and lived-in. Scenes are wide and bright, with a sky above terraces and gardens. Illustrations are full of small details of daily life. Graphic layouts put content in rounded, framed panels on a light ground, with generous space.
  • Matte, handmade surfaces. Flat colour, painted or drawn by hand, with thin dark outlines. Wood, clay, woven fabric, and patched textiles. No gloss, chrome, glass blur, or drop shadows.
  • Humanist and Art Nouveau lettering. Friendly humanist sans-serifs and readable serifs in mixed case. Display lettering can borrow Art Nouveau curves. Wide-spaced capitals and monospace terminal type belong to cyberpunk and other styles.
  • Slow, natural motion. In animation, wind in leaves and sails, turning turbines, and moving light, as in the Chobani “Dear Alice” advertisement (2021). There are no glitches or flicker.

What connects the references

Provisional: no reference records exist yet. The grammar comes from the sources in the attestation. The style-references skill should collect open-licensed concept art, the Solarpunk flag on Wikimedia Commons, and photographs of planted buildings.

Identity

Name

Also called
Solar punk
Era
2014–present. Wikipedia: the term was coined in a 2008 blog post, “From Steampunk to Solarpunk”, and a visual artist’s concept art on Tumblr in 2014 started the aesthetic. Jay Springett’s reference guide (2017, updated 2018) says the early discussions happened on Tumblr from 2014 after Miss Olivia Louise’s character concept post. The style is still current: the Encyclopedia of Science Fiction added an entry in 2024 and updated it in April 2026.

Lineage

  • Influenced by Art Nouveau. Wikipedia: whereas steampunk uses Victorian aesthetics, solarpunk uses more Art Nouveau style and looks to the future. The Aesthetics Wiki lists Art Nouveau and stained-glass solar panels among its key motifs.
  • Influenced by Arts and Crafts. Wikidata records the Arts and Crafts movement as an influence (P737), and Wikipedia says solarpunk shares elements with it. The shared trait is the value of handmade, repairable things, more than the dense flat pattern.
  • Influenced by Organic architecture. Wikidata records organic architecture as an influence (P737). Architizer (2022) and the Aesthetics Wiki describe solarpunk buildings as towers and houses wrapped in planted terraces, with curved forms and visible renewables.
  • Reaction against Cyberpunk. Wikipedia calls solarpunk the inverse of cyberpunk: bright, with light as a motif, against cyberpunk’s dark, artificial city. Wikidata names it after cyberpunk (P138) and records it as based on cyberpunk (P144).
  • Related to Frutiger Aero. The Aesthetics Wiki lists Frutiger Aero as related and compares solarpunk with its offshoot Frutiger Eco: both show green, optimistic technology, but Frutiger Eco is glossy, corporate, and stock-photo-like, while solarpunk looks hand-touched and lived-in.
  • Related to Hopepunk. Wikidata records hopepunk as said to be the same as solarpunk (P460). Hopepunk is a literary mood without a visual grammar of its own, so it stays outside the catalogue.

Classification rubric

The test for a new reference

Identifies the style

  • Plants grow over buildings or objects, and solar panels, wind turbines, or sails are visible among them.
  • The palette is bright and sunlit: leaf green, sky blue, and sun gold on white or cream.
  • Arched windows, domes, or greenhouses, often glazed in stained-glass panes.
  • Surfaces are matte and handmade, with flat colour and thin dark outlines.
  • The scene is daylit, and people live, garden, or repair things in it.

Rules it out

  • Night scenes, neon, rain, and chrome. That points to cyberpunk.
  • Brass, gears, sepia, and Victorian dress without plants or renewables. That points to steampunk.
  • Glossy gradients, water bubbles, and glass highlights. That points to Frutiger Aero.
  • Earthy, muted colours on parchment with no technology. That points to Art Nouveau.
  • Dark ground with violet and bioluminescent light. That points to lunarpunk.

Often confused with

Art Nouveau
Solarpunk borrows Art Nouveau curves and stained glass, but its colours are bright and sunlit (leaf green, sky blue, sun gold) and its scenes show renewable technology and the future. Art Nouveau colours are earthy and muted on parchment, and it shows plants, women, and peacocks, not machines.
Frutiger Aero
Both show green, optimistic technology with sky and plants. Frutiger Aero (and its offshoot Frutiger Eco) is glossy and corporate: gradients, glass, bubbles, and water drops. Solarpunk is matte, drawn by hand, and lived-in, with visible repair and gardening.
Arts and Crafts
Arts and Crafts shares the value of handwork, but its pattern is a dense, flat, symmetrical repeat in deep dye colours with square frames. Solarpunk is open and sunlit, with bright colours and arched panels.
Cottagecore
Cottagecore shows a pastoral past: cottages, baking, and linen, without technology. Solarpunk shows the future and puts solar panels and turbines in the garden.
Steampunk
Steampunk uses Victorian dress, brass, gears, and sepia, and looks to the past. Solarpunk uses green, gold, and sky, and looks to a sustainable future.
Lunarpunk
Lunarpunk is the night side of solarpunk: a dark ground, violet and blue light, and bioluminescent plants. Solarpunk is a daylit style on a light ground.

Ideas to carry forward

  • Use a white or warm cream ground with three colour families: leaf green, sky blue, and sun gold.
  • Keep colours bright and clear, stronger than earth tones and weaker than neon.
  • Frame key content in arched or domed panels, like a greenhouse or a window.
  • Fill one or two panels with a stained-glass grid of cells in green, gold, and blue, as a solar panel drawn in leaded glass.
  • Outline panels and buttons with a thin deep-green line, and keep surfaces flat and matte.
  • Set text in a humanist sans-serif or a readable serif in mixed case.
  • Show plants and visible, simple technology together: leaves, a sun, a turbine, a sail.

Keep the function

  • Do not use a dark ground, neon colours, or glitch effects. That points to cyberpunk.
  • Do not use glossy gradients, glass blur, bubbles, or drop shadows. That points to Frutiger Aero.
  • Do not use brass, gears, or sepia. That points to steampunk.
  • Do not mute every colour to earth tones on parchment. That points to Art Nouveau.
  • Do not use stepped corners, chevrons, or sunbursts in metallic colours. That points to Art Deco.
  • Do not use solarpunk imagery as a green veneer for a product that is not sustainable. Critics call this greenwashing.

Useful directions: community gardens, food co-ops, and repair cafés, renewable-energy cooperatives and climate organizations, speculative-fiction magazines, anthologies, and indie games, festivals, maker spaces, and education about sustainability.

Poor fits:

  • Oil, gas, mining, and fast-fashion brands. The style promises ecological change, so it reads as greenwashing.
  • Banking, legal, and security products that must look neutral and serious. The illustrative, hopeful tone can look naive.
  • Dense dashboards and developer tools. Arched panels and patterns take space and compete with data.
